**Research note: PostgreSQL limits relevant to schema and pool sizing**

PostgreSQL caps identifier length at 63 bytes by default. The lexical structure chapter of the current manual states that the server uses no more than NAMEDATALEN minus one bytes of an identifier, and since NAMEDATALEN defaults to 64, the effective maximum is 63 bytes (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-syntax-lexical.html). Two details matter for us. First, longer names are not rejected but silently truncated, so two long names that share their first 63 bytes collide. Second, the limit is in bytes, not characters, so non-ASCII names in UTF-8 run out of room sooner. The limit can only be raised by changing the constant and recompiling, which is not an option on managed services. The limits appendix repeats the same figure of 63 bytes for identifier length (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/limits.html).

A table can have at most 1,600 columns. The limits appendix lists 1,600 columns per table and 1,664 columns in a result set (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/limits.html). The same page explains that the practical ceiling is lower because every stored tuple must fit in a single 8192-byte heap page. Its own example is that 1,600 four-byte int columns fit, but 1,600 eight-byte bigint columns do not. Dropped columns still count toward the limit until the table is rebuilt, and large variable-length values are moved out of line to TOAST so only an 18-byte pointer stays in the tuple. For a normal service schema none of this should bind, but it is worth knowing if anyone proposes a very wide denormalized table or runs many add-and-drop column migrations.

The default for max_connections is 100. The connections and authentication section of the server configuration chapter says the default is typically 100 connections, but may be lower if kernel settings cannot support that number, as determined during initdb (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-connection.html). The parameter can only be changed with a server restart. The same page notes that PostgreSQL sizes several resources, including shared memory, directly from this value, so raising it has a real cost, and a standby must have a value equal to or higher than its primary. Older documentation versions mirrored by Crunchy Data give the same default of 100 for 9.2 and 9.5, so this default has been stable for many releases (source: https://access.crunchydata.com/documentation/postgresql95/9.5.4/runtime-config-connection.html).

Note that a few of the 100 slots are held back for superusers by the separate superuser_reserved_connections setting, so an application should budget for slightly fewer than the configured maximum. A managed provider may also set a different default based on instance size, so check the actual value with SHOW max_connections on the target instance.

Recommendation: keep every identifier comfortably under 63 bytes with a consistent naming convention, and keep tables far below 1,600 columns by normalizing wide entities. Size the application pool so that all service replicas together stay well under the instance's max_connections minus the reserved superuser slots, and put PgBouncer or a similar pooler in front if the replica count makes that impossible.

{"answers": {"1": "63 bytes (NAMEDATALEN 64 minus 1)", "2": "1,600 columns per table (further limited by the 8192-byte page)", "3": "100 (typically; may be lower if the kernel cannot support it)"}, "sources": {"1": ["https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-syntax-lexical.html", "https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/limits.html"], "2": ["https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/limits.html"], "3": ["https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-connection.html"]}}

**Research note: PostgreSQL memory and WAL defaults**

Before touching postgresql.conf on the new install, it helps to know what the server starts with. I looked up the three settings you asked about in the current official PostgreSQL documentation, and the defaults are conservative enough that you will almost certainly want to raise all three on any machine with more than a couple of gigabytes of RAM.

The first setting, work_mem, sets the base amount of memory a single query operation such as a sort or hash table may use before it spills to temporary disk files. The documented default is four megabytes, written as 4MB, and the docs note that a value given without units is interpreted as kilobytes (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-resource.html). Keep in mind that this is a per-operation limit, not a per-connection or per-server one. A complex query with several sorts and joins can consume many multiples of work_mem at once, and many concurrent sessions multiply that again, so raise it with the connection count in mind rather than simply setting it to something large.

The second setting, shared_buffers, controls how much memory the server dedicates to its shared buffer cache. The documentation states that the default is typically 128 megabytes, written as 128MB, but it may be lower if the kernel settings discovered during initdb cannot support that amount (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-resource.html). That default dates from an era of much smaller machines. The same page recommends starting around a quarter of system memory on a dedicated database server, since PostgreSQL also relies on the operating system page cache and larger values see diminishing returns.

The third setting, max_wal_size, limits how much write-ahead log can accumulate between automatic checkpoints. The documented default is 1 GB (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-wal.html). This is a soft limit, so the server can exceed it under heavy load or when wal_keep_size and replication slots hold segments back. A small value forces frequent checkpoints, which increases write amplification from full-page writes and slows bulk loads. Raising it spreads checkpoints out, at the cost of more disk space under pg_wal and a longer crash recovery window.

All three values come from the versioned "current" documentation pages, which track the latest major release, so if your fresh install is an older major version it is worth confirming against the matching docs page. The practical lesson is that the shipped defaults are tuned so PostgreSQL starts anywhere, not so it performs well on your hardware.

**Recommendation.** For a dedicated server, start by setting shared_buffers to roughly 25 percent of RAM, raise max_wal_size to several gigabytes if the workload is write-heavy and disk allows, and increase work_mem modestly, for example to 16 to 64 MB, after estimating peak concurrent operations. Then watch checkpoint frequency in the logs and temp file usage in pg_stat_database before tuning further.

**Research note: analytics side-store next to PostgreSQL, and MERGE on PostgreSQL 15**

You asked three concrete questions before picking between DuckDB and SQLite as an analytics side-store, and whether PostgreSQL 15 gives you MERGE. All three answers below come from the official documentation pages I read today.

**DuckDB's default memory limit.** DuckDB's operations manual lists the engine's limits in a table, and the row for memory use says the default is 80% of the system's RAM. The setting that controls it is `memory_limit`, and the page notes that this cap applies only to the buffer manager, so other allocations made by the process are not bounded by it (source: https://duckdb.org/docs/2.0/operations_manual/limits.html). For a side-store that lives on the same host as PostgreSQL, that default is aggressive. You will want to lower it explicitly so that DuckDB does not compete with the PostgreSQL shared buffers and OS page cache.

**Maximum SQLite database file size.** The SQLite limits page derives the maximum file size from the maximum page count, which is 4,294,967,294 pages. With the default page size of 4096 bytes that gives a maximum database size of about 17.5 terabytes. With the largest page size of 65,536 bytes, the file can grow to about 281 terabytes (source: https://www.sqlite.org/limits.html). The same page notes that in practice the filesystem or disk will usually run out long before SQLite's own ceiling matters. So the file-size limit should not be the deciding factor for an analytics store of any realistic size.

**When MERGE arrived in PostgreSQL.** The PostgreSQL 15 release notes list "Support for the SQL MERGE command" as the first highlight in the overview. The detailed entry under utility commands describes it as a command "to adjust one table to match another" and says it is similar to INSERT ... ON CONFLICT but more batch-oriented (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/15/release-15.html). So MERGE first shipped in PostgreSQL 15, and your 15 instance has it. Note that in 15 MERGE has limitations that later versions relaxed, such as no RETURNING clause and no support for updatable views, so check the 15 reference page if you plan to rely on those.

**Fit for the side-store role.** DuckDB is a columnar, vectorized engine built for analytical scans and aggregations, and it can read Parquet and CSV directly, which makes it the natural choice for reporting queries pulled out of PostgreSQL. SQLite is a row store designed for transactional and embedded workloads, and while its size ceiling is generous, its query engine will not match DuckDB on wide aggregations over tens of millions of rows. The main operational cost of DuckDB is the memory default above, which you should pin to a fixed value in the connection configuration.

**Recommendation.** Choose DuckDB for the analytics side-store, and set its memory limit explicitly to a value that leaves PostgreSQL enough headroom on a shared host. Use PostgreSQL 15's native MERGE for your upsert-style synchronisation into the primary database, keeping in mind that RETURNING on MERGE is not available until a later major version.

{"answers": {"1": "80% of RAM", "2": "about 281 terabytes (with 65536-byte pages; about 17.5 TB at default 4096-byte pages)", "3": "PostgreSQL 15"}, "sources": {"1": ["https://duckdb.org/docs/2.0/operations_manual/limits.html"], "2": ["https://www.sqlite.org/limits.html"], "3": ["https://www.postgresql.org/docs/15/release-15.html"]}}

**Research note: TLS 1.3, DNS label length, and HTTP 418**

**TLS 1.3.** TLS 1.3 was specified in RFC 8446, "The Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Version 1.3", published August 2018 as a Proposed Standard (source: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8446). One thing worth flagging for the guideline: the RFC Editor now marks RFC 8446 as obsolete, superseded by RFC 9846 (source: https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc8446). RFC 9846 carries the same title, is also a Proposed Standard, and obsoletes RFC 8446 together with the TLS 1.2 specification RFC 5246 and several related RFCs (source: https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9846). The protocol version is unchanged, so "TLS 1.3" still means the same wire protocol, but the current normative reference is RFC 9846. Nearly all existing literature and tooling still cite RFC 8446, which is why both numbers belong in the guideline.

**DNS label length.** RFC 1035, the core DNS specification, sets the limits in its section 2.3.4 "Size limits": a label is "63 octets or less", and a full name is "255 octets or less" (source: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1035). The limit follows from the wire format, where the label length byte has two bits reserved for compression pointers, leaving six bits and thus a maximum of 63. Note the unit is octets, not characters. For internationalized host names the limit applies to the ASCII-encoded A-label form, which can be considerably longer than the Unicode text the user sees. Any host-naming rule in the guideline should therefore say "63 octets per label, 255 octets per name" and apply it to the encoded form.

**HTTP 418.** The status code "418 I'm a teapot" is defined in RFC 2324, "Hyper Text Coffee Pot Control Protocol (HTCPCP/1.0)", section 2.3.2, which states that any attempt to brew coffee with a teapot should result in the error code 418 and that the resulting entity body "MAY be short and stout" (source: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2324). RFC 2324 was an April Fools' document and 418 was never part of the HTTP specification itself. Mozilla's MDN reference confirms the origin in RFC 2324 and adds that RFC 9110, the current HTTP semantics specification, formally reserved the code because of its wide deployment as a joke, so it cannot be given non-joke semantics for the foreseeable future (source: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status/418).

**Recommendation.** Cite RFC 9846 as the current TLS 1.3 reference with RFC 8446 noted as its predecessor, and state DNS limits as 63 octets per label and 255 octets per name measured on the encoded form. Treat 418 as a reserved, non-standard code and forbid its use in production APIs, pointing to RFC 9110 for the authoritative list of status codes.

{"answers": {"1": "RFC 8446 (August 2018; now obsoleted by RFC 9846, published 2026, same title)", "2": "63 octets per label (255 octets for a full name)", "3": "418 I'm a teapot, defined in RFC 2324 (HTCPCP/1.0), section 2.3.2; reserved by RFC 9110"}, "sources": {"1": ["https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8446", "https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc8446", "https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9846"], "2": ["https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1035"], "3": ["https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2324", "https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status/418"]}}

**Research note: platform timing and network defaults for the deploy runbook**

Each value below was checked against the primary source today.

**1. AWS Lambda maximum invocation timeout: 900 seconds.** The Lambda developer guide states that the timeout defaults to 3 seconds and "you can adjust this in increments of 1 second up to a maximum value of 900 seconds (15 minutes)". The console form likewise accepts a value between 1 and 900 seconds (source: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/configuration-timeout.html). One caveat worth a footnote in the runbook: the same page says that functions on AWS Lambda Managed Instances allow up to 5,400 seconds for asynchronous and event-source-mapping invocations, so the 900-second ceiling applies to standard Lambda and to synchronous calls.

**2. Kubernetes Pod default termination grace period: 30 seconds.** The Pod lifecycle concept page says "By default, all deletes are graceful within 30 seconds" and, in the termination flow section, "The default `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` setting is 30 seconds" (source: https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-lifecycle/). After the kubelet sends SIGTERM, the container has that window to shut down before SIGKILL. The value can be raised in the Pod spec or lowered on a specific delete request.

**3. Docker default bridge (docker0) subnet: 172.17.0.0/16.** The Docker docs do not spell the default out as a sentence. The standalone networking tutorial shows a container on the default bridge with the address 172.17.0.2/16 on eth0, and a second container at 172.17.0.3 (source: https://docs.docker.com/engine/network/tutorials/standalone/). The authoritative source is the Moby engine code, where the local-scope default address pool list begins with the entry 172.17.0.0/16, split into /16 networks, and the default bridge is allocated from the first entry (source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/moby/moby/master/daemon/libnetwork/ipamutils/utils.go). The bridge driver page confirms the subnet is overridable with the bip option in daemon.json, so a host with a customised daemon may differ (source: https://docs.docker.com/engine/network/drivers/bridge/).

**Recommendation.** Set a single application-level shutdown and request budget that fits inside the tightest platform limit, so the service drains within 30 seconds on Kubernetes and finishes any one unit of work well under 900 seconds on Lambda, and raise terminationGracePeriodSeconds explicitly if drain takes longer. For local Docker, document that the default bridge uses 172.17.0.0/16 and tell developers on VPNs that overlap this range to set bip in daemon.json before running the stack.

{"answers": {"1": "900 seconds (15 minutes)", "2": "30 seconds", "3": "172.17.0.0/16"}, "sources": {"1": ["https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/configuration-timeout.html"], "2": ["https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-lifecycle/"], "3": ["https://raw.githubusercontent.com/moby/moby/master/daemon/libnetwork/ipamutils/utils.go", "https://docs.docker.com/engine/network/tutorials/standalone/"]}}

Good enough: the 6.1 release notes say "This release adds support for the Rust programming language", and LWN describes 6.1 as "the introduction of support for the Rust programming language". Writing the note now.

**Research note: three tooling defaults, verified against primary sources (2 Nov 2026)**

**Vitest per-test timeout.** Vitest's `testTimeout` option sets the default wait for a single test before it is marked as failed. The current configuration reference states the default is 5,000 ms when running under Node.js, and 15,000 ms when browser mode is enabled (source: https://vitest.dev/config/testtimeout). So unless we opt into browser mode, every test gets five seconds by default. For a repository that runs integration-style tests against a database, five seconds is often too tight once CI machines are under load, which is why teams usually raise it per project rather than scattering per-test overrides.

**First mainline Linux kernel with Rust.** The initial Rust infrastructure landed in Linux 6.1, released in December 2022. The KernelNewbies release summary for 6.1 states plainly that "This release adds support for the Rust programming language" and adds that "This release includes some initial support for Rust, which will be improved in later releases" (source: https://kernelnewbies.org/Linux_6.1). LWN's coverage of the 6.1 merge window describes the same pull as "the introduction of support for the Rust programming language" into the mainline kernel, and notes that the merge was deliberately minimal, with only a sample module and no real drivers (source: https://lwn.net/Articles/910762/). The practical point for us is that 6.1 is the historical floor, not a sensible target. The Rust toolchain requirements and in-kernel abstractions changed heavily in later releases, and the current kernel Rust documentation is published against 7.x (source: https://docs.kernel.org/rust/index.html). If the team wants to "follow a kernel version for Rust", it should track a recent stable or LTS series rather than pin to 6.1.

**PostgreSQL statement_timeout.** The PostgreSQL client-connection configuration reference documents `statement_timeout` as aborting any statement that runs longer than the given amount of time, and states that "A value of zero (the default) disables the timeout" (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-client.html). In other words, a stock PostgreSQL server never kills a long-running statement on its own. The same page notes the timeout can be set per session or per role, and the manual advises against setting it globally in `postgresql.conf` because it would also hit maintenance operations such as backups and `VACUUM`.

**Recommendation.** Set an explicit `testTimeout` in the vitest config (a value like 10,000 to 20,000 ms for suites that touch a database) and set `statement_timeout` on the application role or connection string rather than leaving it at the server default of zero. For Rust-in-kernel work, treat 6.1 as the historical starting point only and standardise on the most recent LTS kernel series the team's toolchain supports.

{"answers": {"1": "5000 ms (Node.js; 15000 ms with browser.enabled)", "2": "Linux 6.1", "3": "0 (disabled)"}, "sources": {"1": ["https://vitest.dev/config/testtimeout"], "2": ["https://kernelnewbies.org/Linux_6.1", "https://lwn.net/Articles/910762/"], "3": ["https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-client.html"]}}
